scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Nati originated in the Western and Central Hills of the Indian subcontinent as a community tradition native to Himachal Pradesh, with historical roots across Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, Sirmaur, Chamba, and Kinnaur.
Historically danced exclusively by male villagers, women have increasingly become the primary practitioners sustaining the form.
Due to regional migration of pahari communities, the dance has also established popularity across the plainlands.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Nati is performed across community and religious celebrations, including births, weddings, harvest gatherings, and major festivals such as Diwali and Dussehra.
The dance draws thematic meaning from Vaishnava devotional narratives of Raaslila and Chandravali.
When held as part of sacred religious events, dancers conclude the performance with a formal yagna fire ritual to honour local Hindu deities.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers arrange themselves in open circles or semi-circles without participant limits, moving forward and backward in coordinated lines.
Performers either hold hands with alternate partners to form a criss-cross pattern or sway their hands freely through the air, turning their palms into a horizontal figure-eight motion.
Group lines are led by male dancers brandishing a fly whisk (chowrie) or an axe (dangru).
Watch for Criss-cross Handhold, Horizontal Figure Eight Palm Sway, Basic 8-Step Footwork.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Performances are accompanied by traditional musicians known as tunis, playing regional percussion and wind instruments.

The rhythmic core is maintained by dhol, damau, and nagara drums, complemented by the melodic tones of the shehnai and brass wind instruments including the longish karnal horn and curved narsingha (narsinghe).
Listen for the dhol, damau, nagara, shehnai.

A resonant mountain ensemble dominated by the pulse of dhol, damau, and nagara drums, punctuated by piercing reedy melodies on the shehnai and the long, ringing calls of brass karnal and curved narsingha horns.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes vary by district across Himachal Pradesh.

Male attire includes Himachali topis (caps), fitted woollen suthan trousers, kurtas, Nehru jackets, and gachi waist sashes, with Kinnaur dancers adorning topis with flowers and Indian trumpet seeds, Sirmaur men wearing choltu tunics, and Kullu men wearing flower garland headwear.
Women wear suit-salwar or rezta dresses, sadri vests, dhattu headscarves, and regional jewellery including chandrahaar, bumni, and jhanjhar, with Kullu women donning pattu drapes.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dr. Joginder Singh Habbi directed the Sirmour District cultural group, achieving ten consecutive folk dance competition victories and entering Sirmouri Natti into the India Book of Records, Asia Book of Records, and the World Book of Records.
Distinct regional forms include Kullvi Nati, Mahasuvi Nati, Sirmauri Nati, Kinnauri Nati (noted for mime-like, languid sequences), Jaunpuri Nati, Barada Nati, and Bangani Nati.

Nati's expressive choreography is rooted in narratives of the Hindu deity traditions of Raaslila and Chandravali, carried forward across generations in the Himalayan valleys through family, festive, and village temple gatherings.
